deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematical derivation on this page. It is part of Riemann's epistemological fragment 'Versuch einer Lehre von den Grundbegriffen der Mathematik und Physik, als Grundlage für die Naturerklärung'. The page continues the opening sentence from folio 4r/Blatt 6 and runs as follows.

(1) Concepts determine future perceptions. The concepts through which we grasp nature fill in our present perceptions. They also predetermine future perceptions: as necessary where the conceptual system is complete enough, otherwise as probable. They fix what is (really) possible, and hence what is necessary, meaning its opposite is impossible. If the concepts are precise enough, the degree of possibility ('probability') of each possible event can be determined mathematically. This is a programmatic statement that probability is a measure over the space of events the theory allows. Nothing is computed.

(2) Confirmation and revision. If what the concepts make necessary or probable actually occurs, the concepts are confirmed. Our trust in them rests on such confirmation by experience. If something occurs that the concepts make impossible or improbable, the task arises to supplement or, if necessary, rework the conceptual system. The aim is that, under the completed or corrected system, the observation ceases to be impossible or improbable. This supplementation or correction constitutes the 'explanation' of the unexpected perception. Through this process our view of nature becomes gradually more complete and more correct. At the same time it reaches ever further behind the surface of appearances.

(3) Historical claim. The history of the explanatory natural sciences shows that this is indeed how knowledge advances. Marginal insertion: the present conceptual systems arose by gradual transformation of older ones. The reasons that drove science to new modes of explanation can always be traced to contradictions or improbabilities that showed up in the older ones. Hence the formation of new concepts, so far as it can be observed, happens through this process.

(4) Herbart against Kant. Herbart has shown that the concepts used for our view of the world can all be derived from this same source. This applies even to concepts whose origin we cannot trace, either in history or in our own development, because we receive them unnoticed with language. It holds so far as they are more than mere forms of combining simple sensory representations. Therefore, the sentence completed on the next page says, they need not be derived, as Kant's categories are, from a constitution of the human soul presupposed prior to all experience.

This text was published, with editorial smoothing, by Weber and Dedekind in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke, in the section 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts', under 'Erkenntnisstheoretisches'.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics. The philosophical claim that Herbart 'proved' the empirical origin of all world-concepts is Riemann's partisan endorsement, not an established result.
The claim that probabilities can be 'mathematically determined' from a sufficiently exact conceptual system is asserted without any specification of the measure.

results.what: Scientific concepts fix what is possible and necessary and assign probabilities to events. Theories are confirmed when predictions occur and revised when improbable or impossible events occur; this revision is what 'explanation' means.
results.modern_name: Hypothetico-deductive / probabilistic confirmation view of science; theory revision driven by anomaly (proto-Popperian/Kuhnian/Bayesian themes)
results.usually_credited_to: Broad 19th-century tradition (Herschel, Whewell, Mill, Helmholtz); later Popper, Kuhn

results.what: Endorsement of Herbart's empirical-psychological derivation of fundamental concepts, against Kant's a priori categories.
results.modern_name: Herbartian empiricist psychology of concept formation

deep.surprise_reason: Purely philosophical text, already published in Riemann's Gesammelte Werke (Erkenntnisstheoretisches) and well known to Riemann scholars as evidence of his Herbartian orientation. It contains no mathematics.
